Females of Southern hake reach sexual maturity at a total length of 74.7 cm [Lp = 74.7 cm], a size that is attained after several years of growth in the cold, productive waters of the Patagonian shelf. The body mass at this pubertal transition has been estimated at 2554 grams [Wwp = 2554 grams], derived from length-weight relationships established for the species. This milestone marks the onset of gonadal activity and the beginning of the adult phase, during which individuals join the spawning aggregations that occur along the continental slope. The maximum size documented for this species is 155 cm [Li = 155 cm] in total length, representing the asymptotic length approached by the oldest and largest individuals in the population. Such a size is considerable among members of the Merlucciidae and reflects the productive foraging conditions in the Subantarctic region. The corresponding ultimate body mass for an individual of this length is substantial, reaching up to 24542 grams [Wwi = up to 24542 grams] according to empirical growth models fitted to capture data. These morphometric benchmarks provide critical reference points for stock assessment and management, as they define the reproductive and somatic potential of the population.

At the commencement of life, each fertilised ovum develops within a small, transparent chorion, and newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are minuscule, weighing only 0.0007 grams [Wwb = 0.0007 grams] upon eclosion. This neonatal mass is derived from an average egg diameter of 1.1 mm, illustrating the limited maternal investment per offspring in this batch-spawning gadiform. The early larval phase is entirely lecithotrophic, with the alevin subsisting on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days post-hatching. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs rapidly after mouth opening, a critical transition that determines survival in the planktonic environment. The shift from an endotrophic to an exotrophic state is a period of high mortality, as the tiny larvae must encounter suitable prey items within a narrow temporal window. The initial wet weight of 0.0007 grams [Wwb = 0.0007 grams] is among the lowest recorded for commercially important finfish in the Southern Ocean, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritises high fecundity over large egg size. This early-stage size constraint has profound implications for larval dispersal and recruitment success in the species.

A mature female Southern hake is capable of producing a remarkable number of offspring during a single spawning season. Field studies indicate that a ripe female can carry a batch fecundity of approximately 8.2 million hydrated oocytes, which, when released in a single annual spawning event [F_R_i = single annual spawning event], results in a maximum daily reproduction rate of 22,466 oocytes per day [Ri = 22,466 oocytes per day] when maintained at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This estimate is derived from a relative fecundity of 334 oocytes per gram of somatic tissue, applied to the ultimate body mass of 24542 grams. The individual is capable of releasing this entire clutch in a single spawning event, thus achieving the maximum reproductive output per event. The investment is substantial, with these oocytes comprising a significant proportion of the female's body weight at spawning. Such high fecundity is typical of broadcast-spawning marine teleosts that experience high larval mortality. The maximum reproductive output for this species, combining the large clutch size with a single annual spawning event, represents a prodigious allocation of energy toward the next generation.

The longevity of Southern hake is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals reaching a lifespan of 10,950 days [am = 10,950 days], which corresponds to approximately 30 years in the wild at a temperature of 8.6 °C [T = 8.6 °C]. This estimate was derived from tagging and otolith-based ageing studies conducted in the cold waters of the South Pacific, at a mean annual temperature of 8.6 °C [T = 8.6 °C]. This extended lifespan is consistent with the slow growth rates and delayed maturation characteristic of many high-latitude fish species. The species exhibits a type III survivorship curve, where mortality is extremely high during the early larval stages but declines substantially after the juvenile period. The maximum recorded age of 30 years [am = 30 years] places Merluccius australis among the longer-lived members of its genus, a trait linked to the low metabolic demands of its cold-water habitat at a temperature of 8.6 °C [T = 8.6 °C]. This longevity has important implications for population dynamics, as it confers a degree of resilience to fishing pressure through multiple overlapping year classes. However, it also means that recovery from overexploitation can be slow due to the protracted pre-reproductive period.

The ultimate body mass of 24542 grams [Wwi = 24542 grams] for Southern hake is reached only after decades of growth in the species' preferred thermal regime. The length-weight relationship for this species, calculated as weight equals 0.00398 times total length raised to the power of 3.10, demonstrates a slightly positive allometric growth pattern, indicating that individuals become relatively heavier for their length as they age. This allometric shift is likely related to the accumulation of lipid stores in the musculature and liver, which serve as energy reserves for reproduction and overwintering. In contrast, the pubertal body mass of 2554 grams [Wwp = 2554 grams] represents a critical threshold that is reached relatively early in life, at a size far below the asymptotic maximum. Females at this stage are yet to achieve the full somatic growth potential of the species, but they are already reproductively viable. The disparity between pubertal and ultimate body mass highlights the substantial post-maturation growth that characterises this iteroparous species, allowing individuals to increase their fecundity with each successive spawning season as body size and ovarian capacity expand.
